title: Sudan’s Power Grid on Brink of Collapse Following Wave of Strikes Targeting Electricity Stations
author: Aunnab Alman

Al-Mashkour Ali stands beside his grain mill at the Al-Lafa market in south
Khartoum on November 16, 2026. Prolonged power outages following recent drone
strikes on Sudan's electricity infrastructure have forced him to work alone
overnight during the limited hours electricity is available. Photo by Aunnab
Alman.

KHARTOUM, Sudan--In what has become an increasingly frequent feature of daily
life in large swathes of Sudan, Afifa Mohammed spent most of Tuesday in her
small home in Al-Asal south of Khartoum without electricity. The power went
out at 10 a.m. and did not return until close to midnight.

Like millions of other Sudanese displaced by the country's brutal civil war,
Mohammed was forced to flee her hometown of Bara, North Kordofan, with her
children in March. Added to the hardship of displacement, she now has to
contend with a lack of electricity.

She stays awake late into the night when power is available and rushes to
complete tasks that require electricity--like pumping and storing water. The
family now buys small quantities of food daily because they can no longer
depend on refrigeration. There is no reliable schedule of power cuts. Some
days, electricity comes on during the day before cutting out after sunset.
Other days, the pattern is reversed.

Sudan's electricity network has been severely damaged over the last three and
a half years of war with civilian infrastructure being targeted by both the
Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Yet a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and
into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity
infrastructure has brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse.
The United Nations children's agency (UNICEF)
[warned](https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/drones-and-drought-sudan-
combined-assault-children-nothing-seen) recently that not a day had passed
during the last week of October without a drone striking a power station in
Sudan.

"In just over two weeks between October 20 and November 4, 29 drone strikes,
attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel
stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further
fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines," the
United Nations Human Rights Office said in a
[statement](https://sudan.un.org/en/326318-un-report-details-deadly-civilian-
impact-surge-drone-strikes) this week. "These drone strikes had a devastating
impact on civilians and essential services, causing power outages that
disrupted health services including dialysis and surgical procedures, access
to clean water and food production."

Two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remain out of service.
Repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take
months or longer, Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity
Company, told Drop Site News.

Across parts of the country, electricity is being rationed through planned
cuts that do not adhere to a regular schedule, while hospitals, water systems,
farms, and businesses struggle to operate on an already weakened grid.
Replacement transformers must be manufactured abroad, spare parts are scarce,
and the threat of further attacks is complicating efforts to restore power.

Ismail said the recent wave of attacks damaged some of the most difficult and
expensive components to replace, including high-capacity transformers and
digital control systems. Unlike smaller electrical equipment, the transformers
cannot be purchased from local suppliers and instead must be manufactured to
order in Europe or Asia to match the specifications of individual power
stations. Manufacturing, shipping, and installation can take several months to
more than a year, he added, particularly when equipment must be transported
through a country torn apart by war.

A single large transformer can cost millions of dollars while Sudan's
electricity authorities face shortages of foreign currency, Ismail said.
Additional shortages in essential supplies, including cables, circuit
breakers, and insulating oil, have exacerbated the crisis while reserve stocks
have been depleted following the destruction of major warehouses in Khartoum.

The Sudanese military-backed government has accused the RSF of carrying out
attacks on electricity infrastructure, and the UN also cited the RSF regarding
the latest wave of strikes. While both warring parties have targeted civilians
and committed human rights abuses, the RSF has been accused of the most
serious crimes, including actions in the group's takeover of El Fasher in 2025
that bore "the hallmarks of genocide," according to a UN Independent
International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan.

The conflict erupted in April 2023 when a long simmering rivalry between the
two factions exploded into fighting. At least 150,000 people have been killed,
with some estimates running far higher. Some 14 million have been forced from
their homes and the International Rescue Committee says more people face
famine in Sudan than in the rest of the world combined.

As the war between the SAF and the RSF continues to rage, the threat of
renewed attacks has created another obstacle to restoring the power grid.
According to Ismail, foreign companies and potential international donors are
reluctant to finance repairs or send specialist engineers into areas where
installations could be struck again.

One of Sudan's most important power stations, the Um Dabakir thermal power
plant in White Nile State, was badly damaged in an October 29 strike that
forced it to shut down. The station supplied major parts of White Nile and
North Kordofan states, supported the wider grid serving Khartoum and Al-
Jazirah, and provided electricity used by water-treatment facilities,
hospitals, and agricultural projects, Ismail said.

Communities around Kosti, Rabak, and Al-Obeid, including large numbers of
people displaced by the war, depend on services connected to the affected
network. Restoring the station would require four replacement main
transformers, reconstruction of its control room and electrical feeders, and
maintenance of three damaged generating units, according to Ismail. He
estimated that the repairs would cost tens of millions of dollars and take at
least several months.

In Khartoum, the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was also put out of
service following a strike on October 27. The facility is a major connection
point for electricity transmitted from Merowe Dam to Omdurman, Bahri, and
parts of the capital. Its disruption also affected water infrastructure and
hospitals connected to the network. Initial estimates suggested repairs could
be completed within 10 days. But Ismail said the damage required imported
transformers, high-voltage insulators, and other equipment unavailable
locally. Affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and
scheduled power cuts as of this week.

The Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy have yet to
publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the
attacks. On November 15, distribution transformers were installed to restore
supplies to Khartoum's Central Market and Local Market. But these localized
interventions have not resolved the wider damage to the transmission network.

## **Effects Ranging from Dialysis to Agriculture**

At Abdullah Sheikh Al-Jumaih Hospital in Dongola, Northern State, power cuts
have interrupted patients during dialysis treatment. Dr. Rasha Abdullah, a
physician at the hospital, told Drop Site that a power cut in early November
caused at least one dialysis machine's electrically powered blood pump to stop
functioning, leaving blood in the tubing and filter at risk of clotting before
it could be returned to the patient. Abdullah scrambled to use the machine's
manual emergency mechanism to return the blood to the patient's circulation.

"The medical situation in the Northern State is critical, as hospitals rely on
electricity for up to 98 per cent of their equipment and lighting," Abdullah
said. She added that the power cuts have also disrupted the hospital's
medicine storage.

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5ff82b1-96d7-4f1c-8bd0-ff0f0ed9a2af_576x576.jpeg)Haemodialysis
machines inside the Al-Asil Center in Dongola, Northern State, Sudan on
November 19, 2026. During sudden power cuts this month when backup power
failed, medical staff were forced to manually hand-crank the machines' blood
pumps to return circulating blood to patients before it clotted, while power
outages also forced the center to discard refrigerated stocks of essential
anti-clotting heparin. Photo courtesy of Dr. Rasha Abdullah.

During one prolonged outage, the hospital's refrigeration systems stopped
functioning for an entire day. With no alternative available, staff were
forced to discard quantities of heparin, a medication used to prevent blood
clotting during dialysis, because they could no longer ensure that the
affected supplies had been stored under the proper conditions, Abdullah said.

Attacks on power infrastructure are also disrupting water supplies. "The right
to water deteriorated significantly, particularly as prolonged electricity
cuts, fuel shortages, attacks on infrastructure and disruptions to water-
pumping systems affected access to safe drinking water," the UN Human Rights
Office said in a recent report.

Workers and farmers across the economy are being affected by repeated
blackouts.

At Al-Lafa market, south of Khartoum, grain mill owner Mohammed Al-Mashkour
Ali said that after the recent wave of attacks, electricity in his area was
available only between midnight and 7 a.m. He has taken to working alone at
night, grinding as much grain as possible before customers arrived the
following day.

"During the day, the electricity is completely cut off," Ali said. "Customers
come to buy grain and have it ground, but I am unable to meet their demands."

He initially tried using a small generator, but rising fuel prices made it too
expensive to operate. "In the early days, I tried relying on a small
generator, but the rise in fuel prices caused me financial losses with little
return, so I stopped," he said.

In Al-Jazirah State, farmer Sahar Mohammed said electricity shortages had
disrupted the processing of agricultural products, even in areas where
irrigation does not depend directly on the national grid. Mills and oil-
processing facilities rely on electricity, while the cost of operating diesel-
powered alternatives has increased. In Northern State, farmer Abu al-Qasim
Muhammad Ahmad said the shutdown of the Al-Daba substation had left his area
on an alternating electricity schedule: one day with power, followed by one
day without it. He said the irregular pumping has damaged his alfalfa and
orange crops.

Farmers who switched to diesel-powered irrigation faced higher costs and fuel
shortages. Ahmad estimated that his production costs had doubled. He feared
that continued disruptions would affect preparations for the winter growing
season, particularly for crops of wheat and fava beans.

Sudan's electricity network had suffered extensive damage before the intense
wave of drone strikes that began in late October. Before the latest attacks,
national generation capacity had fallen from approximately 4,400 megawatts
before the war to around 1,100 megawatts, according to the Associated Press.

Merowe Dam is now the last major power source in the country, providing more
than 70% of the country's electricity and making transmission facilities that
distribute its output to other parts of the country even more critical.

Ismail estimated that approximately 70% of Sudan's electricity infrastructure
had been affected by the conflict and that the cost of repairing the wider
network could exceed $3 billion, though he warned the lack of comprehensive
records made it difficult to establish the full extent of the destruction. The
recent attacks have compounded that damage by disabling facilities that
distribute electricity between regions.

According to Ismail, areas still connected to the grid are relying on load-
sharing arrangements and emergency rerouting of electricity. Some communities
receive power on alternating days, while others experience prolonged scheduled
and unscheduled cuts.

In parts of White Nile, North Kordofan and other areas dependent on severely
damaged facilities, outages can last considerably longer.

Introducing alternative energy systems, including solar power, would reduce
the dependence of hospitals and agricultural projects on the national grid.
Yet those systems also require financing, equipment, and maintenance at a time
when Sudan's public institutions are struggling to fund even basic repairs.

"A worrying trend is the recent intensification of drone strikes targeting
power stations and fuel supply," the UN Human Rights office said this week.
"The parties to the conflict must protect civilians and uphold their
international law obligations--the world is watching," said UN High
Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
